raw_segments.text: Rarity in our age, Cartesius, as he himself often enough repeats, did not doubt with respect to faith.
Memores tehmen, ut jam dictum est, Huic lumini naturale tambiutantum esse credendum,
quamdu nile contrarium adio ipso revelator.
Præter cetera autumn, memori nostri pro summa regula est infigendum, equinabis adio revelata sunt,
ut omnium certissima esse credenda, et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maxime clarem et evidens,
alliud quid nobis sugerer vydredder, soli taman octoritati divinipodius quam proprianostro judicio
phidum esse adheibendum, CFR, Principia philosophy, pars prima section 28 and section 76.
He did not cry fire and make it a duty for all men to doubt, for Cartesius was a quiet,
solitary thinker, not a bawling street watchman. He modestly confessed that his method had
significance only for himself, and was grounded in part in his own earlier botched learning.
Niquis ichiter putet, mi hich traditurum alliquem methodum, quam anusquisque seque debit ad rect
regendum rationum, elam anim tantum, quam ipsemit secutus sum, exponer de crevi.
